At the opening, Yin Tongyue, Chairman of Chery Automobile Co., Ltd., declared a somewhat familiar statement: This year, we will boldly proclaim that Chery's global innovation system will also 'not hold back.' In 2024, Chery's global passenger vehicle sales totaled 74.3 million units, ranking among the world's top 20 automakers with 2.295 million units sold and achieving the highest year-on-year growth rate of 49.4% on the list. Additionally, Chery has gained significant presence in overseas markets, covering 120 countries and regions with over 5.5 million cumulative users, and it has led China's passenger vehicle exports for 22 consecutive years. In 2025, its PHEV models ranked first in market share in eight countries, including Chile, the UAE, and Thailand, with projected sales in the European market reaching 80,000 units. However, in today's highly competitive market, Chery clearly cannot afford to relax. At this conference, Chery introduced five core technology areas: Mars Architecture, Kunpeng Power, Lingxi Smart Cabin, Falcon Intelligent Driving, and Galaxy Ecosystem. At the architectural level, Mars Architecture serves as an underlying platform covering all brands and powertrain types, flexibly adaptable for sedans, SUVs, MPVs, and crossovers, with core technologies focused on electronic architecture and chassis systems.

excerpt_i18n.en: In 2025, the AI community finally shifted from "large model worship" to "application realism." As the parameter race among foundational models like Baidu's ERNIE, Alibaba's Tongyi, and Tencent's Hunyuan subsided, and the "hundred-model war" evolved into "industry-wide applications," companies suddenly realized that computing power, once considered mere infrastructure, had become the decisive factor in application deployment. The issue wasn't a lack of computing power, but the inability to find "just-right" computing power; not insufficient computing power, but wasted resources from "misallocated" computing power; not unaffordable computing power, but the cost of "ineffective usage" eroding profits. Oracle's $300 billion computing power deal with OpenAI also signaled industry changes: this wasn't merely "selling computing power" but an "ecosystem partnership." OpenAI requires Oracle's massive-scale computing clusters to support GPT-5's training and inference, while Oracle secures its computing demand for the next decade by aligning with a leading model company. This reflects two core trends in the global computing power market: first, "computing demand shifting from concentration to explosion." Large model training demands immense computing power (GPT-5 requires 10 times the computing power of GPT-3), while inference for applications like multimodal systems and AI agents grows exponentially. For instance, a live-streaming AI controller handling video streams, speech recognition, and audience interaction simultaneously consumes vastly more inference computing power than ordinary tasks.
